$comment: The manual-validation ledger: every check a machine cannot run, how to run
it, and where its result went.
Automated gates are self-recording — CI is either green or it is not. The
checks that need a phone, a mushaf, or a pair of ears have no such memory:
they get done once, written into a decision record in prose, and then nobody
can answer 'is that still true, and on what device, and when?' without
reading four documents. This file is that answer, in one place a gate can
read (scripts/gate-validation.mjs).
The point is not bookkeeping. It is that a manual result should end up
tightening something automated — a threshold, a fixture, a new gate — so the
expensive check does not have to be repeated to stay true. That is what the
`tunes` field records: what this verdict is allowed to change. An entry whose
`tunes` is empty is a check we are paying for and not banking.
status:  pending | done | superseded
blocks:  roadmap items that cannot proceed until this is `done`
tunes:   the automated artifact this result feeds (threshold, fixture, gate)
staleAfterDays: for repeating checks — how long a `done` result stays valid
before the gate asks for it again. Omit for one-shot checks.
runbook: the check, written so someone holding a phone and no memory of the
conversation can run it. This is the ONLY place a runbook is
written; three renderers read it and nothing else restates it:
make validate CHECK=<id>   → the terminal
make guide                 → docs/validation/guide.html, on the phone
the `validate` skill       → drives a session end to end
Shape:
needs   — what you must have before starting (a device, a print, a deploy)
setup   — [{run, expect}] commands run here, on the laptop
steps   — [{do, expect, why, shot?, id?}]
do     — the action
expect — what should happen if it is working. A step with
no expectation cannot be failed, so it cannot be
passed either.
why    — what this step buys. An expectation you cannot
justify is one a tired reader will wave through.
shot   — id of a screenshot in docs/validation/shots/,
captured from the real app by `make shots`, never
hand-cropped. Only where a picture answers a
question the prose cannot: what the screen looks
like before you have ever seen it. The gate fails
on a `shot` with no file behind it.
id     — a name for this step, so `evidence.covers` can
point at it. Optional: give a step an id when
something automated discharges it. Never a
position — a reordered runbook must not silently
re-point a claim about which step is done. (The
comments in e2e/share-a11y.spec.ts said 'Runbook
step 4' and had been wrong for two loops.)
reading — how to turn what you saw into a verdict; one line per outcome
record  — the exact command that banks the result
A `pending` check owned by `user` with no runbook.steps fails the
gate: a check nobody can follow is a check that will not be run, and
it should not be able to sit here looking tracked.
evidence: the machine half of this check — one command, what it discharges,
and what it cannot. Optional, and most of the checks here
deliberately have none: a producer that does not exist must not be
invented, and a runbook that already absorbed its automation into
the step text (screen-reader-walkthrough) has nothing left to strike.
run     — the command. NOT a `make` target: GNU make reports every
failed recipe as exit 2, which flattens a producer's own
1-vs-3 (a verdict vs 'could not tell') into one code, and
a timeout would then read as a finding.
covers  — runbook step ids this run discharges. `make validate-auto`
runs the command and writes the real exit code to
docs/validation/evidence/<id>.json; the terminal and the
guide strike those steps ONLY on a pass. Exit 3 means
'could not tell' and strikes nothing — an automated run
that could not reach its subject has proved nothing.
residue — what the command cannot do, in words. REQUIRED, and the
reason the field is safe: this is the one place in the
register that takes work away from a human, so it has to
say out loud what is left. An `evidence` with no residue
is a claim to have automated a manual check entirely,
which has never once been true here.
The evidence record's path is derived from the check id, not stored:
a path written down twice is a path that can disagree with itself.

checks.title: On-device pan/zoom + highlight-toggle verdict
checks.why: The emulated baseline (~8.3 ms/frame, flat under CPU throttle) structurally cannot see the two real risks: initial raster of a ~170 KB inline SVG on a low-end phone, and re-raster on zoom past the layer's backing store. The rendering-scale decision for 604 pages rests on this and nothing else.
checks.how: make phone-perf → open the printed LAN URL on a real mid/low-tier Android and an older iPhone → tap ابدأ and follow the bar for 15s (pan, pinch, tap ayahs) → long-press the JSON it prints and paste it into this entry's `result`. No cable and no DevTools: the phone measures itself with a rAF sampler (apps/web/src/perf/probe.ts), because the old recipe — pair over USB, enable Web Inspector, find the timeline — is why this check sat open for six loops. Run it twice where you can, once as a browser tab and once from the Home Screen install; the JSON stamps which. The DevTools route still works if you want a flame chart: `make phone` serves the same build without the probe.
checks.decides: inline-SVG everywhere | content-visibility virtualization | raster-glyph fallback

needs: A real phone on the same Wi-Fi as this laptop — a mid/low-tier Android and an older iPhone if you have both; either one alone still answers most of it.
No cable, no DevTools, no pairing. The page measures itself.
About 3 minutes per device.

setup.expect: Builds a throwaway probe bundle, prints `On your phone (same Wi-Fi): http://<lan-ip>:4173`, then holds the terminal open serving it. Leave it running.

steps.do: Open that URL on the phone.
steps.expect: The mushaf page as normal, plus a dark slab pinned across the top reading «قياس الأداء على هذا الجهاز — ١٥ ثانية» with an ابدأ button. No slab means you are on an ordinary build — something else is already serving port 4173; stop it and re-run make phone-perf.
steps.why: Confirms you are measuring the build that has the probe in it. An ordinary build looks completely normal, which is exactly how you would not notice — and every number below would then be a measurement of the wrong thing.

steps.do: Tap ابدأ.
steps.expect: «استعد / get ready» for one second before each segment, then the segment's instruction and a countdown. The slab ignores taps while recording, so you cannot accidentally drive it instead of the page.
steps.why: The one-second «استعد» beat is there so the tail of one gesture does not land in the head of the next segment. Rush it and the three numbers blur into each other, which is the one way this check can fail without looking like it failed.

steps.do: Segment 1 — «مرّر الصفحة بإصبع واحد»: pan the page with one finger, continuously, for the whole 5-second countdown.
steps.expect: The page moves under your finger and the counter runs 5→1. Keep moving: a still finger produces no frames and the segment will report «too few frames — not driven».
steps.why: Pan is the cheap case: no re-raster, just compositing a layer that already exists. If pan is over budget then nothing further matters — the page is too heavy as DOM and the verdict is raster-fallback.

steps.do: Segment 2 — «قرّب وباعد بإصبعين»: pinch in and out, going far enough that glyph edges visibly re-sharpen.
steps.expect: Zoom follows the pinch. The re-sharpen moment is the one being measured — it is the layer being re-rastered.
steps.why: This is the whole check. Zooming past the layer's backing store makes the browser re-rasterize ~170 KB of glyph paths, and that cost is structurally invisible to the emulated desktop baseline. The rendering decision for all 604 pages turns on this one number.

steps.do: Segment 3 — «اضغط آيات مختلفة»: tap a different ayah roughly once a second.
steps.expect: Amber marker swipes land on each ayah you tap — one along the middle of every line it occupies, with the scripture still readable through them. Different ayahs, not the same one twice — you are measuring overlay churn.
steps.why: Separates rendering cost from interaction cost. If only this segment is bad the problem is overlay churn in the highlighter — a real bug, but not one that changes which rendering strategy Loop 4b builds.

steps.do: Read the results table, then long-press the JSON box → Select All → Copy.
steps.expect: «النتيجة — الصقها في ledger.json», a row per segment with mean / fps / p95 / worst / jank (over-budget cells in salmon), and a read-only JSON blob stamped with the device, dpr, cores, standalone flag, build commit, and FCP/LCP. There is no copy button on purpose: a LAN preview is plain http, so the Clipboard API does not exist here.
steps.why: The table gives you the verdict; the JSON is what makes it re-checkable a year from now. It stamps device, dpr, cores, standalone flag and build commit, so a later reader can tell whether the number still describes the phone in their hand.

steps.do: If you can, add the site to the Home Screen and run the whole thing again from there.
steps.expect: `"standalone": true` in the second JSON. Standalone gets its own compositor path on iOS, so the two runs can legitimately disagree — that difference is a result, not noise.
steps.why: iOS gives standalone its own compositor path. If the two runs disagree, the install prompt is doing load-bearing work rather than convenience work — and that changes what Loop 6b has to guarantee.

reading: p95 ≤ 16.7 ms and jank < 10% on all three segments → verdict **inline-svg**: inline SVG everywhere holds, and Loop 4b is plain vendoring + streaming.
Pan fine but pinch p95 much worse → re-raster past the layer's backing store → verdict **content-visibility**: virtualize off-screen pages; do not rasterize glyphs.

Pan itself over budget, or worst > 100 ms on the first pinch → the page is too heavy as DOM → verdict **raster-fallback**: rasterize the glyph layer, keep the polygon hit layer as DOM (the highlighter API does not change).
Only the tap segment is bad → that is INP, not rendering: overlay churn in packages/core/src/highlighter.ts. It does not change the rendering verdict; file it separately.
«too few frames — not driven» on any segment → that segment never got a real gesture. Re-run it; a number from an undriven segment is not a result.
The two devices disagree → the low-end one decides. The budget exists for the phone that struggles.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=perf-verdict-on-device RESULT='inline-svg — Pixel 6a p95 14/23/9 ms (pan/pinch/tap), jank 6/18/2%; iPhone SE similar' — then paste the full JSON into docs/decisions/loop-4b.md

tunes: apps/web/perf/pan-zoom-trace.mjs — the frame budget asserted in CI becomes the measured number, not the emulated one
docs/PLAN.md §Loop 4b — which of the three rendering strategies gets built

checks.title: VoiceOver / TalkBack gesture walkthrough
checks.why: axe and the keyboard hop tour cover the machine-checkable floor and are green, but neither can tell you whether a screen-reader user can actually select an ayah and hop. Per-polygon labels are a design bet that has never been heard out loud.
checks.how: On the same phone as perf-verdict-on-device: enable VoiceOver (iOS) / TalkBack (Android), then run the core tour by gesture alone. The accessibility tree — which controls exist, in what order, under what names — is pinned in apps/web/e2e/__aria__/ and re-checked on every run, so this check is now only the three things a runner cannot do: judge the phrasing by ear, try to escape a sheet by gesture, and do the whole tour without looking.

needs: The same phone, with VoiceOver (iOS: Settings → Accessibility → VoiceOver, or triple-click the side button) or TalkBack (Android: Settings → Accessibility).
About 8 quiet minutes. You are listening, not looking — the last step asks you to stop looking entirely.
The ordinary build, not the probe build.

Nothing to memorise. This used to be eight steps; five of them were checking that a control existed under a given name, and those are now aria snapshots in apps/web/e2e/__aria__/{iphone,android}/ that fail the build when a label changes. Reading those five files first is optional and takes a minute — they are exactly what the app should announce.

setup.expect: Prints `Open on your phone (same Wi-Fi): http://<lan-ip>:4173` and serves the normal app — no perf slab at the top.

steps.do: Turn the screen reader on, open the URL, swipe into the mushaf, and listen to three or four ayah labels in a row. Judge the phrasing out loud. This is the bet under test.
steps.expect: «الآية البقرة · ٢:٤٨» — that the label exists and reads exactly this is already asserted by e2e/__aria__/*/page-group.aria.yml. What you are judging is whether it sounds like something you would say, and whether your voice speaks ٢:٤٨ correctly rather than as "two colon four eight" or as a year.
steps.why: The one thing no linter can check. axe proves a label exists and the snapshot proves it has not changed; only an ear can tell you the phrase is one a person would use, and only a real voice engine tells you how Arabic-Indic digits actually come out.

steps.do: Double-tap an ayah with hops, open a rail chip, and try to escape the sheet: swipe past the last item, and swipe backwards past the first. Then hop to a target and immediately swipe once.
steps.expect: Both swipes stay inside the sheet — neither walks you into the page behind it. After the hop, the next swipe lands on something real on the new page, not on a node from the sheet that no longer exists.
steps.why: Focus containment and focus survival across a page change are the two failures that make hopping unusable without sight, and neither is visible to a runner: the tree is correct in both the working and the broken case. The sheet's own contents — «إغلاق», «انتقل إلى …» — are pinned in e2e/__aria__/*/hop-popover.aria.yml and are not what you are checking here.

steps.do: Now do the whole tour with the screen off or your eyes closed: find an ayah, hop, come back along the trail.
steps.expect: You can do it. Whatever you could not do — or could only do because you already knew where things were — is the result of this check.
steps.why: Every label can be correct and the app still unusable, because you knew where to swipe. This is the actual verdict; the two steps before it are how you find out why it failed.

reading: A label that reads awkwardly, or digits your voice speaks wrongly → change the label in packages/core/src/highlighter.ts (enhancePolygons) or the component that owns it, then regenerate the aria snapshots (`pnpm -C apps/web exec playwright test share-a11y --update-snapshots`) and read the diff — it is the new announcement, written down.
Focus escaping a sheet, or stranded after a hop → an e2e assertion, not a label change. The tree is already correct in both cases, which is exactly why this half stayed human.

A control announced in the wrong order or not at all → that is a snapshot failure and should have failed CI before you picked up the phone. If it did not, the surface is missing from the aria-snapshot set — add it to apps/web/e2e/share-a11y.spec.ts.
A tour you could complete but found exhausting → write that in `result` anyway. Feel is not a bug report, but it is exactly what this check can see and axe cannot.
Nothing wrong at all → say which reader, which OS version, and which phone. A pass on VoiceOver 17 is not a pass on TalkBack.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=screen-reader-walkthrough RESULT='VoiceOver iOS 17 on iPhone SE — full tour by gesture; ayah labels read «الآية البقرة · ٢:٤٨» (fine); rail chips read as words; one finding: <…>'

tunes: apps/web/e2e/__aria__/ — the pinned trees. Delivered ahead of this check (2026-07-27); a phrasing verdict lands here as a regenerated snapshot, which is the announcement written down
apps/web/e2e/share-a11y.spec.ts — a surface with no snapshot yet, or a focus behaviour you could break, becomes a test there
packages/core/src/highlighter.ts — the aria-label shape, if the labels read badly

checks.title: Read the Complex's published terms at the source
checks.why: SOURCES.md currently reads KFGQPC's terms through quran-svg's NOTICE.md, which quotes them verbatim and cites Royal Decrees 136/8 and 9/B/46356 — strong, but secondary. The app states those terms to every reader in the colophon, and an earlier paraphrase of them was wrong.
checks.how: Open qurancomplex.gov.sa in an ordinary browser. The host is unreachable from automation, and this was measured rather than assumed: a GitHub-hosted runner (Azure westus2, run 30285643491, 2026-07-27) resolves the A record to 66.9.131.70 and then times out on TCP 443 — connect rc=124, and curl returns 000 under both a curl and a desktop-Chrome User-Agent. The same failure appears from the maintainer's machine. Two unrelated networks failing at the TCP layer is not a bot filter a header could talk past, and web.archive.org is not fetchable from the tooling either, so no scheduled watcher can do this. It stays a human check permanently. Confirm the wording still says free digital/web/software use with commercial printing reserved.

needs: An ordinary browser, outside this environment — ideally one on a residential connection, since two datacentre/office networks have now failed to reach the host. It resolves and then times out on TCP 443 from both a GitHub runner in Azure westus2 and the maintainer's machine, and the Wayback mirror is not fetchable from the tooling either. That is the entire reason this is a human check, and the reason no watcher will ever be built for it.
About five minutes.

steps.do: Open https://qurancomplex.gov.sa/en/ and find the terms / digital publications page.
steps.expect: It loads. (It does not load from this repo's tooling, which is why nobody has read it yet.)
steps.why: The primary source, not a mirror. Every licensing claim this project makes about the glyph corpus currently rests on a third party's summary, and a summary is precisely where a restriction gets softened.

steps.do: Read what it says about reusing the digital mushaf.
steps.expect: Free use in digital, web and software contexts, with **commercial printing of physical masahif** reserved to the Complex — the same restriction quran-svg's NOTICE.md quotes, citing Royal Decrees 136/8 and 9/B/46356.
steps.why: What is at stake is whether the reserved right is commercial printing of physical masahif or something broader. Those two readings put this project in very different places.

steps.do: Confirm our two restatements say the same thing as each other — SOURCES.md §hafs-kfqc and the colophon's «الرخصة والمصدر».
steps.expect: They agree on the substance. `pnpm gate:license-copy` asserts this on every commit, so you should only have to read one of them in the next step.
steps.why: Two copies of someone else's licence terms drift silently, and the drift is the defect: a stranger reading the app and a stranger reading the repo would be told different things about what they may do. Delegating this to a gate is what makes the next step a comparison against ONE restatement rather than a three-way diff.

steps.do: Compare that against the two places we restate it: SOURCES.md §hafs-kfqc, and the colophon in the app (tap the wordmark حِفظ → «الرخصة والمصدر»).
steps.expect: Both should describe free digital use with the printing restriction — and specifically NOT «إتاحة حرّة للاستعمال غير التجاري» (non-commercial only), which is a different edition's term and shipped once as a live defect.
steps.why: We restate these terms in two places a stranger can read, so a wrong restatement is a licensing claim we are making on the Complex's behalf. This exact string was wrong once and shipped.

reading: Wording matches what we say → drop the 'pending that glance' clause from SOURCES.md's Status line. Nothing in the build changes.
Wording has moved → change SOURCES.md AND apps/web/src/components/Colophon.tsx together; they are the same claim in two places.

You are unsure whether our summary is stricter than the source → treat that as a failure and write it down. Overstating someone else's terms fails silently: it reads as caution, so no reader ever files a bug about being told they have fewer rights than they do.
The Libyan Endowments editions (Qālūn/Warsh) really are non-commercial-only — do not let their terms drift back onto this row.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=kfgqpc-terms-primary-source RESULT='read at qurancomplex.gov.sa/en/ on <date> — free digital use, commercial printing reserved; matches SOURCES.md and the colophon'

tunes: SOURCES.md §hafs-kfqc — drops the 'pending-that-glance' clause from the Status line
apps/web/src/components/Colophon.tsx — the mushaf licence line, if the wording moved

residue: Reading qurancomplex.gov.sa itself. The host times out on TCP 443 from every network this project's tooling runs on (measured, twice) and the Wayback mirror is not fetchable either — that is why research ⑦ was cancelled rather than built, and why no watcher will ever cover this.

Judging whether our summary is **stricter** than the source. A gate can prove two copies match; only a reader can notice that both are wrong in the same direction, and overstating someone else's terms fails silently because it reads as caution.

checks.title: The GPL §6 offer resolves for a stranger
checks.why: Publishing a static PWA conveys it: the browser receives real copies of the JS and of assets/roots/**, a GPL-covered derivative. The colophon links SOURCE_REPO at the exact build commit, which discharges the obligation only if that URL opens for someone who is not signed in as us.
checks.how: Open the colophon's source link in a private/logged-out browser window against the deployed build. It must land on real source, at a commit, not a 404.

needs: Two minutes of network. `make source-offer` follows the same links anonymously and answers the machine half before you pick up a phone.
The **deployed** build, not localhost. The question is what a stranger receives, and localhost cannot answer it.
A private / logged-out browser window — signed in as ourselves, a private repo looks public.

setup.expect: A verdict, printed. `source-offer — OK` → every link already resolves anonymously and what is left below is confirming the *reader’s* path to them. `DOES NOT RESOLVE` → it names which link failed and why; you can stop here and fix that. `COULD NOT TELL` → the network would not answer, which is not a pass.

steps.do: Open the deployed site in a private window.
steps.expect: The app loads normally.
steps.why: Private, because your own session hides the failure that matters: a link that resolves only because you are signed in does not resolve for the stranger the GPL offer is written for. `make source-offer` has already followed the links with no credentials at all; what it cannot tell you is whether a reader can *get to* them from inside the running app, which is what the rest of this is for.

steps.do: Tap the wordmark حِفظ at the top of the chrome (it announces «عن حِفظ»).
steps.expect: The colophon sheet opens, with a «الرخصة والمصدر» section and a link labelled «الشيفرة المصدرية».
steps.why: The offer has to be reachable from inside the running app, not just from the repository. A colophon nobody can find is an offer that is not being made.

steps.do: Note the short commit printed beside the link, then follow the link.
steps.expect: Real source at that exact commit — a `/tree/<sha>` URL — not a 404, not a sign-in wall, and not a bare branch that moves under the reader. The sha is baked at build time (CF_PAGES_COMMIT_SHA → GITHUB_SHA → git rev-parse HEAD).
steps.why: A bare branch link moves under the reader. The offer is for the source of the binary they are running, and the pinned sha is what makes it a real offer rather than a gesture.

steps.do: Scroll the colophon to the credits and follow one of the attribution links too.
steps.expect: They resolve. The mutashabihat licence asks for a mention in the app; corpus.quran.com's terms require the link.
steps.why: Two of the corpora we build on ask for a link, not merely a mention. A dead attribution link is a licence term being quietly failed.

reading: 404 or a sign-in wall → the §6 offer is not discharged and the site must not be published. Either make the repo public, or repoint SOURCE_REPO in apps/web/src/provenance.ts at wherever the source is actually served.
Lands on the repository root with no commit → the build had no sha available. The offer is weaker but not broken; fix the build environment, not the constant.
Lands on a commit that is not the deployed build → the deploy and the link disagree, which is worse than no link. Check the build-time resolution order.

`make source-offer URL=<deployed>` disagrees with what you see on screen → believe the script about the links and your eyes about the path to them. It reads SOURCE_REPO and the build’s commit out of the deployed bundle, so a disagreement means the page you opened and the bundle it loaded are not the same deploy.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=source-offer-resolves RESULT='private window → colophon → الشيفرة المصدرية resolves to <repo>/tree/<sha>, matching the deployed commit'

tunes: apps/web/src/provenance.ts — SOURCE_REPO, if the source is served from somewhere other than the GitHub repo
scripts/check-source-offer.mjs — if the offer moved, or a new credited source needs its link followed

residue: Whether a reader can *get to* those links from inside the running app. The script follows URLs it reads out of the bundle; it never opens the colophon, so a source link that resolves perfectly from behind a sheet nobody can open still passes it.
Whether the deployed build is the build you think it is. Without `URL=<deployed>` the script answers about this working tree, which is a different question from the one a stranger asks.

checks.result: Repository made public 2026-07-29. Followed anonymously: the repo root, the exact build tree (bc365d3), and all 4 attribution links resolve. GPL §6 discharged; public deploy unblocked.

checks.title: Edge spot-audit — 20 sampled pairs against a printed mushaf
checks.why: The data is scripture. Every automated gate here proves the shards are well-formed; none can prove an edge is true. This is the only check that can, and it is the one whose results are worth the most per minute spent.
checks.how: Draw 20 pairs from the shipped shards — stratified so every kind of edge gets looked at, not just the common kind — look each up in a printed mushaf, and judge whether they are genuinely mutashabihat. Record every verdict — correct AND wrong — in packages/etl/data/qa/verified-edges.json.

needs: A printed mushaf — the KFGQPC Hafs print the pages are photographed from, so page numbers line up. No paper? .claude/skills/mushaf-reference/SKILL.md names the published scans and page tables that stand in, and — more importantly — which ones are a different qira'a or a different print revision and will make a correct pair look wrong.
30–45 minutes for twenty edges. A hafiz if you can get one; this is the check where a second reader is worth the most.
Nothing else — the draw runs here.

setup.expect: Ends with an edge-audit coverage table: one row per class of edge (type × curated-or-dataset × page distance), each marked ✓ or ·. The · rows are the classes nobody has ever looked at — those are what this round is for.

A header naming the edition, the seed, and the rerun command, then twenty numbered **pairs** — `from → to  type  p.<page> / p.<page>  curated|dataset  words <n>  roots <n>/<n>` — then a JSON block ready to paste. Use a fresh SEED per round; add NEW=1 to draw only from pairs no verdict has settled.

steps.do: Work through the twenty pairs in the print, one at a time.
steps.expect: Each `from` and `to` is findable at the page printed beside it. A pair you cannot locate is itself a finding — record it as wrong with a note.
steps.why: This is the only check in the project that can say the data is true. Every other tier verifies that the app faithfully renders whatever the ETL produced — including when what it produced is wrong.

steps.do: Read `words` and `roots` beside each pair as hints, and distrust them.
steps.expect: `words` is the longest run of words the two ayahs share — the same score gate:edges enforces a floor on, computed by the same reader (packages/etl/scripts/morphology.mjs), so a number here can never disagree with CI. `roots` is how many of the shorter ayah's roots appear in both, in order.
steps.why: They point at the pairs worth slowing down on from both ends: a high `words` with a wrong verdict is a plausible-looking false edge, and a low one that is nonetheless right is the case the product exists for — 2:48 → 2:123 swaps شفاعة and عدل, scores 1, and is genuinely confused by huffaz every day.

steps.do: For each, answer the question the tool prints — not «are these similar?» but «**would a hafiz confuse these two while reciting?**»
steps.expect: Most edges are obvious either way in a few seconds. The slow ones are the informative ones; note why.
steps.why: "Similar" is not the standard; a hafiz's confusion is. An edge that is textually close but never actually confused is noise in the rail, and noise is what makes a reader stop trusting the hop.

steps.do: Optionally open a pair in the app to see what a reader actually sees: make phone, then navigate to the ayah and open its rail.
steps.expect: The edge appears as a hop under the direction chip its `type` implies.
steps.why: Catches a correct edge with a wrong presentation. A real mutashabih filed under the wrong direction chip sends the reader looking in the wrong surah, which reads as bad data even though the data is fine.

steps.do: Paste the printed JSON block into packages/etl/data/qa/verified-edges.json under `entries`, setting each `verdict` to `correct` or `wrong`, `verifiedBy` to your name, and `note` where a future reader needs the reason.
steps.expect: Forty entries for twenty pairs — the block writes out both directions of each pair, because every edge in the corpus is generated in both and one reading settles both.
steps.why: Recording the `correct` verdicts matters as much as the failures: they are what turns half an hour of reading into a permanent regression fixture instead of an anecdote.

steps.do: Run pnpm gate:verified-edges.
steps.expect: OK. Those verdicts are now enforced in both directions, forever — a `correct` edge that disappears and a `wrong` edge that returns both fail the build.
steps.why: This is the step where manual work becomes automated. Once it is green, a `correct` edge that disappears and a `wrong` edge that returns both fail the build — forever, without anyone re-reading twenty pairs.

reading: Record BOTH verdicts. A rejected edge that is not written down comes back on the next data refresh and costs the reader's time all over again — and no automated check can tell a wrong edge from a right one.

If several wrong edges share a shape — same `type`, same phrase length, same surah pair — that is a filter in packages/etl/scripts/build-adjacency.mjs, not twenty more rejections. A class of error is worth more than the twenty.
If gate:verified-edges fails later, do not edit the fixture to go green: the data moved under a human verdict. Find out what moved it, and re-verify with a reader before changing a verdict.
This check goes stale after 14 days because the data keeps moving. A fresh seed each round means the coverage accumulates instead of re-checking the same twenty.

Look a pair up by KEY, not by page, in whatever reference you use. Our print is QCF V2/1421H and most published tables are V1/1405H; they place different ayahs on 36 pages, so a page-based lookup in the 583–600 band finds the wrong ayah and the pair reads as wrong data. `make probe-reference ALL=1` asserts that divergence is still exactly the expected 36 and nothing else moved — it settles the arithmetic under this check, and none of the judgement.

Aim at the · rows. The draw is stratified for a reason: 97% of the corpus is one class (dataset mutashabih, far apart), so a flat draw of twenty essentially never shows a shared-root edge, a related-meaning edge, or a pair we curated ourselves — and those are exactly the classes no automated check covers, since gate:edges deliberately does not score shared-root at all. Pass UNIFORM=1 only when the overall *rate* of bad edges is the question, and note that gate:edges already carries the rate on every commit.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=edge-spot-audit RESULT='seed 1 · 20 edges · 18 correct, 2 wrong (both phrase-overlap between 2 and 3) → verified-edges.json'

tunes: packages/etl/data/qa/verified-edges.json — every verdict becomes a permanent gate assertion via gate:verified-edges
packages/etl/scripts/build-adjacency.mjs — a systematic class of wrong edge becomes a filter, not 20 more rejections

residue: Every pair. The gate re-checks verdicts that are already banked against the shipped corpus; it cannot look at a mushaf, and no verdict exists until someone has. This is the one check in the register that can establish the data is true, and it is human by construction.

Choosing what to look at. `make validate` prints which strata have never been audited — a class with no verdict in it is a class where a wrong pair survives every check this repo has — but pointing at the gap is not closing it.

checks.title: 8+ day offline survival, installed vs browser tab
checks.why: Safari's ITP deletes all script storage for origins untouched for 7 days of browser use, and Home-Screen-installed apps are exempt. That single asymmetry is why the install prompt is a feature and not a nicety — and it has never been observed, only read about.
checks.how: Pin a juz in both an installed PWA and a Safari tab. Leave both for 8+ days of normal browser use. Then go into airplane mode and try to revise the pinned juz in each.

needs: **Runnable as of Loop 6b.** The button exists: open the page chip in the header, the sheet «ما فتحتَه من المصحف», the «جزء» scope, then «احفظ الجزء ١ هنا» at the top. Pin **juz 1** in both buckets — it is what the e2e pins, so a discrepancy is comparable against something, and it is ~2.9 MB, which is small enough to re-pin over a masjid connection if the day-8 answer is bad. What is already asserted without a phone — visited pages surviving a reload offline, the app recovering from an eviction, and a pinned juz opening a never-visited page with the radio off — is in apps/web/e2e/offline.spec.ts. All that is left here is the waiting.

**What the eight days no longer have to find.** Research ④ replaced the *eviction* half of this check with `Storage.clearDataForOrigin` over CDP, which takes the origin's caches out from under a live page exactly as a sweep does. That found two real defects (the precache never rebuilt after eviction, so one sweep ended offline support permanently; and a page that failed to fetch left the chrome claiming a page the stage was not showing). Both are fixed and asserted in the `Hifth · eviction` describe. So this check is now only about the thing no harness can supply: whether iOS actually sweeps an uninstalled origin at ~7 days and spares an installed one.
An iPhone (the ITP asymmetry is Safari's), and a deployed build.
Eight days of ordinary phone use. The clock counts days of *browser use*, not calendar days — a phone left in a drawer does not run this experiment.

steps.do: On the phone, open the deployed site in a Safari tab, tap the page chip in the header, choose «جزء», and press «احفظ الجزء ١ هنا».
steps.expect: The button becomes a count («جارٍ حفظ الجزء ١ — ن من ٢٤») with «إيقاف» beside it, and settles into a row reading «الجزء ١ · ٣٫١ م.ب» or thereabouts — the offer disappears, because the juz is now kept. If the row instead says «ناقص» the pin did not finish; press «احفظه من جديد» before starting the clock.
steps.why: The tab is the case we expect to lose. Proving it worked on day 0 is what makes a day-8 failure evidence rather than a guess.

steps.do: Add the site to the Home Screen, open it from there, and pin the same juz again inside the installed app.
steps.expect: Two independent storage buckets now hold the same pack. That is the experiment.
steps.why: Two buckets, same pack, same phone, same eight days. It is the only arrangement that lets you attribute a loss to the storage sweep rather than to the network, the build, or the device.

steps.do: Write down today's date, then use the phone normally for 8+ days. Do not open Hifth in either place.
steps.expect: Nothing. This step is the check.
steps.why: ITP counts seven days of browser use, not seven days of wall clock, and it cannot be fast-forwarded. The waiting is the instrument.

steps.do: On day 8 or later, turn on airplane mode and open the Safari tab: try to revise the pinned juz — open pages, hop, turn pages.
steps.expect: The tab may have lost everything (ITP clears script storage for origins untouched for 7 days of browser use). If it has, the notice «الصفحات التي حفظتها لم تعد في هذا الجهاز» should be on screen with «اعرض المحفوظ» beside it, and under «المحفوظ في هذا الجهاز» the row for juz 1 should read «لم يعد في هذا الجهاز» or «ناقص» — not a broken page, and not a row still claiming megabytes it no longer has.
steps.why: Airplane mode is what makes this a storage test rather than a cache test: whatever still works is genuinely resident on the device.

steps.do: Still in airplane mode, open the installed app and do the same.
steps.expect: The juz is still there. Installed apps are exempt from that sweep — this asymmetry is the whole reason the install prompt is first-class.
steps.why: If the installed app survives and the tab does not, the install prompt stops being a nicety and becomes the feature that makes offline revision real — which is what Loop 6b has to be designed around.

reading: Tab evicted, install survived → the assumption holds. Assert the eviction-detection path in apps/web/e2e/offline.spec.ts and keep the install prompt prominent.
Both survived → note the exact iOS version; the rule may have relaxed. The install prompt's copy then becomes a nudge rather than a warning, which is a copy change, not an architecture one.

The installed app was evicted too → the re-pin offer's trigger in apps/web/src/storage.ts is now urgent rather than theoretical, and the offline story needs rethinking before any 'works offline' claim ships.
Anything showed a broken page instead of an offer to re-pin → that is the bug, whichever bucket it happened in.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=offline-survival-8-day RESULT='iOS <ver>, pinned <date>, checked <date+8> — tab: <evicted|intact>, installed: <evicted|intact>; re-pin offer <appeared|did not>'

tunes: apps/web/e2e/offline.spec.ts — the `Hifth · eviction` describe already asserts recovery against a simulated sweep; tune it to what the phone actually did (which bucket lost what, and whether the shell repair fired before the reader noticed)

apps/web/src/pwa.ts — `repairShellCache()` re-registers `sw.js` under a query-suffixed URL, because a script URL the registration has never seen is the only thing observed to force the install that refills an evicted precache. If iOS evicts differently — registration gone too, or storage back but stale — that trigger is what changes.
apps/web/src/storage.ts — the re-pin offer's trigger, if eviction looks different than assumed

checks.title: Two days of real revision produce two days in the record
checks.why: The revision record is tested against fake-indexeddb in Node, where the clock is a parameter, nothing evicts, and every write lands. All three are false on a phone. Three specific things can only be seen there: whether a write inside a tap gesture survives the app being swiped away seconds later (iOS kills backgrounded tabs aggressively, and the store deliberately writes per tap rather than batching precisely because of that); whether a day boundary in the record matches the day boundary the reader lived through, since `dayOf` files by the offset captured at record time and nothing in CI has ever run under a non-UTC clock; and whether the whole log is still there a week later, given that iOS deletes script-writable storage after 7 days of no interaction — the exact condition a 'what have I not touched in weeks' view exists to report on. A record that quietly resets and says nothing is worse than no record: it tells a hafiz they have revised nothing.
checks.how: Revise on a phone on two different calendar days, at least one session late enough to be near midnight, swiping the app away immediately after some taps. Then read the record back and check the days, the counts and `since`.

needs: A phone — an iPhone if you have one, since the seven-day sweep is Safari's and it is the failure this check is mostly about.
A deployed build, and two calendar days. The second session must be on a different local day from the first; that is the whole point of the first three steps.

**There is no picture yet.** Task #91 is gated on Loop 4b, so the record is read back through the browser's own IndexedDB inspector rather than through a view in the app. Safari: connect the phone to a Mac and use Web Inspector › Storage › Indexed Databases › `hifth.revision.v1`. Chrome on Android: `chrome://inspect` from a desktop, then Application › IndexedDB. The `days` store is keyed by `YYYY-MM-DD`; the `meta` store holds one row, `since`.

**What no harness can supply.** `revision-store.test.ts` proves the retention window, the `since` stamp and per-tap durability against a real IndexedDB implementation, and `App.test.tsx` proves the three exclusions through the real UI. None of that runs under a phone's clock, a phone's storage pressure, or a phone's process killer.

steps.do: Open the deployed site on the phone. Before tapping anything, look at `meta` → `since` in the storage inspector.
steps.expect: A row already exists, stamped with today's local date — written by opening the store, not by any tap.
steps.why: This is the entire defence against the seven-day sweep. A record that has existed for a month and holds nothing means the reader did not tap; one that has existed since this morning and holds nothing means we lost it. If `since` only appeared after the first tap, those two are indistinguishable forever after.

steps.do: Tap five or six ayahs on a page, then drag a marquee across a short passage. Tap one of those ayahs a second time to dismiss it.
steps.expect: Under `days` → today's date: one entry per ayah you selected, exactly one entry for the whole marquee (carrying both a `key` and an `endKey`), and nothing at all for the tap that dismissed.
steps.why: The three exclusions are asserted in App.test.tsx, but against a synthetic pointerup on a fixture page. This is the same claim against a finger on the real gesture stack — where a marquee release and a tap are told apart by @use-gesture, not by the test calling one or the other.

steps.do: Tap two or three more ayahs, then immediately swipe the app away from the app switcher — within a second or two, before anything could plausibly flush.
steps.expect: Reopen and inspect: those last taps are all present.
steps.why: The store writes on every tap instead of batching, which costs a rewrite of the day's array per tap. This step is what that cost is buying. A batched writer loses exactly the taps made just before the app is killed, which on a phone is most of them — and it would have looked perfect in every test in this repo.

steps.do: If you can, do one short session within half an hour either side of local midnight, and note the wall-clock time.
steps.expect: Looks before midnight file under the earlier date and looks after it under the later one — by the phone's own clock, not UTC.
steps.why: Every clock in CI is UTC, so `dayOf` reading the offset from the event has never once been exercised against a real one. Someone revising at 23:40 in a UTC+3 city and again at 00:20 has revised on two days; if the record shows one, the offset is not riding on the event and every evening session east or west of Greenwich is mis-filed.

steps.do: On a later calendar day, open the app again and revise for a few minutes.
steps.expect: `days` now holds two keys, the earlier one unchanged, and `meta` → `since` still shows the first day — it must not have moved forward.
steps.why: `since` moving with the record would make the log look freshly created every time it was read, which is precisely the wipe's signature. This is the cheapest way to catch that, and it cannot be caught at all in a suite that creates a new database per test.

steps.do: Now leave the app alone for eight or more days of ordinary phone use, then open it and look at `days` and `since`.
steps.expect: Either the record is intact, or it is empty **and** `since` reads as today — never empty with an old `since`.
steps.why: This is the failure the feature is designed around and the one no harness can produce: iOS sweeping an origin nobody has touched. The two acceptable outcomes are 'the history is there' and 'the history is gone and the record admits it is one day old'. The third — empty, with a `since` from weeks ago — is the app telling someone they have not revised in a month. Note whether the phone had the site installed to the Home Screen or open as a tab; that is the same asymmetry offline-survival-8-day measures for the page cache, and this is the IndexedDB half of it.

reading: Everything as expected → the record is real on a device. Loop 4b can proceed to task #91 (RevisionMap) on the understanding that the numbers behind the picture are true.
Taps lost after a swipe-away → per-tap durability is not enough on this OS. That is a `recordLook` problem, not a UI one, and it must be fixed before any picture is drawn from the data.

The near-midnight session filed under the wrong day → `tz` is not reaching the event. Everything else in the record is then wrong by up to a day for every reader not on UTC, which is almost all of them.

Record empty with a stale `since` → the store's own defence failed, and no view may render the record until it is fixed. Say what the storage inspector showed; the shape of what survived is the diagnosis.

Record empty with today's `since` → the sweep happened and the record told the truth about it. That is a pass for this check and a hard requirement on #91: the picture must render 'we cannot know' differently from 'you did not revise'.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=revision-record-lands-on-a-phone RESULT='<iOS|Android> <ver>, <installed|tab>, sessions <date> + <date> — per-tap after swipe-away: <kept|lost>; midnight filing: <correct|wrong|not tested>; after 8 days: <intact|empty+fresh since|empty+stale since>'

tunes: apps/web/src/revision-store.test.ts — the retention and `since` tests are written against a clock passed in as a parameter. Whatever the phone actually did to the log gets a case here, in the units the phone reported it in.
packages/core/src/revision.test.ts — the DST/offset cases were reasoned about, not observed. Replace the invented offsets with the real one from the near-midnight session.

packages/core/src/revision.ts — `RevisionEvent`'s doc comment lists what must not become an event. If the phone shows a gesture this repo did not anticipate producing a look, that list is what changes.
apps/web/src/revision-store.ts — if a swipe-away loses taps, the per-tap write is not sufficient and the durability comment at the top of the file is currently a claim rather than a fact.
docs/map.json → revision-record — the `extend` steps for task #91 depend on which of the two acceptable outcomes actually happens at day eight.

checks.title: Placement correction by eye — a hundred forced choices between the corrected box and the one we ship
checks.why: The measurement says nearly every mark rectangle sits about a letter away from its own ink, and that one number per page fixes it. Only arithmetic has ever said so, and it marked its own homework: the rasteriser that found the displacement is the rasteriser that scores the correction. Nobody has looked at a single verdict. Until somebody does, the thresholds in the placement record stay unenforced, and nothing that points at a mark can ship — which is the whole reason to hold three hundred thousand rectangles. And the hundred trials are drawn from pages the correction was never fitted on, because a correction asked about the pages it was fitted to answers a question nobody needed: it will ship on all six hundred and four.
checks.how: Work a hundred two-panel trials by eye. Each shows the same mark twice with one rectangle drawn on it, and asks which rectangle sits on the mark. Usually one of them is the corrected placement and the other is what the app draws today; nothing on the screen says which, and no answer key is written anywhere — the scorer rebuilds it from the seed afterwards. Save the ruling the page hands back, score it, and bank the verdict.

needs: Both printings on this machine: the pages the app ships, and the gitignored ligature cache the mark boxes are read from. If the placement measurement has ever run here, they are already present; if not, the first setup command says so and stops.
About twenty minutes, in as few sittings as you can manage. A hundred trials is roughly thirteen minutes of looking; the rest is settling in.
A screen you are not squinting at, and no opinion about what the answer ought to be. Nothing else — no mushaf, no phone, no network.
Nobody has to be a hafiz for this one. It is a question about where a rectangle sits, not about what the mark says.

tool.label: The hundred trials
tool.note: Built by the setup command. Opened from here, every answer you give lands in this session's transcript as you give it; opened as a file on its own, it keeps its own copy and hands you a download at the end. Either way it says nothing about how you are doing, because it does not know.

setup.expect: A line reading 40 of 600 measured, 40 held out · even, then a hundred trials over forty pages in about a second, and two short fingerprints — one for the corrections, one for the pages. Note both. It writes the page and a companion file of the same name ending .pages.json. Open the page in any browser: it needs nothing running and it reaches no network.

steps.do: If you are also going to sit the placing session, sit this one first.
steps.expect: Nothing to run. It is an order, not a command.
steps.why: The placing session shows the same rectangles and invites you to drag them onto the mark, which is the most effective possible way to learn where our correction tends to sit. Come to these hundred trials afterwards and you are answering from that lesson rather than from the ink, and the count that comes out is a measure of how well you learned it. The reverse order costs nothing: knowing which of two rectangles you preferred does not tell you where to drag anything.

steps.do: Read the five short answers the page opens with, then start. Do not read the code that built it first.
steps.expect: A first trial: one mark, drawn twice side by side, a rectangle on each, and two keys.
steps.why: The trials are built so that nothing on the screen says which rectangle is ours, and the answers exist nowhere until the scorer runs. Reading the builder first is the one way to spoil that, and there is no way to unspoil it — the session would have to be thrown away and rebuilt under a seed you had not seen.

steps.do: For each trial pick the panel whose rectangle sits on the mark — A or B — or press space when you honestly cannot tell.
steps.expect: No feedback, ever: the next trial, and a bar creeping along. Some pairs are obvious. Most are not, and a few are the same rectangle twice, where space is the only honest answer.
steps.why: Feedback would turn this into training. Within twenty trials a person who is told they were right learns which way the corrected box tends to sit and answers from that rule rather than from the ink, and the count that comes out measures how well they learned it. Space is not a wasted trial: it is left out of the arithmetic rather than counted as a miss, so guessing to keep the tally up is the one thing that would cost you.

steps.do: When the mark pokes out of both rectangles, press N to say neither closes around it — and then still pick whichever of the two is closer.
steps.expect: The tick lights up and clears itself on the next trial. It changes nothing else on the screen, and it never skips the trial.
steps.why: A rectangle can be in the right place and still be the wrong size, and this whole session is about where they sit. Those are two faults with two different repairs, so a fourth button meaning 'wrong somehow' would blend them into one count nobody could act on — and it would eat the trials that still carry a usable answer, because which of two wrong rectangles is closer is a question you can answer. The tick is counted on its own line and the marks you tick are named, so somebody can go and look at those boxes rather than argue about whether they exist.

steps.do: Stop whenever you are tiring. Close the tab and come back to the same file later.
steps.expect: It resumes on the trial you left, with the answers you already gave. Nothing reshuffles.
steps.why: Pushing through a hundred trials tired means the last thirty are answered from fatigue, and in the numbers fatigue is indistinguishable from 'the correction does not help' — it would read as a finding about our data rather than about the hour.

steps.do: At the end, press the button that saves the ruling, and keep the file somewhere you can name on a command line.
steps.expect: mark-ruling-11.28042a4d.json in your downloads. It holds your answers, the seed, and both fingerprints — and no key, because there still isn't one. The second half of the name is the page list: two sittings under this seed that asked about different pages are different sittings, and without it they arrive in the same folder as the same file.
steps.why: The ruling is deliberately worthless on its own. That is what makes it evidence: it could not have been edited towards an answer, because at the moment it was written nothing on the machine knew what the answers were.

steps.do: Score it: pnpm adjudicate:score ~/Downloads/mark-ruling-11.28042a4d.json --shift docs/validation/rulings/mark-shift.604pages.c849e72d.json
steps.expect: Four lines with intervals — as shipped, the decoy, the catches, twins — then, if you ticked any, how many marks poked out of both rectangles and the headline again without them. One sentence of verdict at the end. It exits 0 only when the session was valid and the corrected rectangle actually won.
steps.why: This is the first moment anyone knows what the right answers were, you included. The corrections have to be named because the ones sitting loose in the build directory are whatever was measured last, and this sitting was built from a particular committed file. If it refuses outright, that is the two of them disagreeing: score against the file it was built from, or build a fresh session and work it again. A ruling scored against corrections it was not worked against comes out looking clean and means nothing.

steps.do: Bank the verdict with the record command below, whichever way it went.
steps.expect: The ledger gains the four numbers and the date, and this check stops being pending.
steps.why: A refusal is worth as much here as a confirmation and is far more likely to be dropped on the floor. 'A person looked and did not prefer our correction' is the single most valuable sentence this project could learn about the mark layer, and it is unrecoverable a week later if nobody wrote the numbers down.

reading: 'The correction is supported' → adopt the per-page displacement. The two numbers per page get recorded beside the fit, and the measurement's thresholds become something a gate is allowed to enforce, which is the change this check unlocks.

'NOT supported, and the decoys say why' → the strongest result this can produce, and the reason it is worth twenty minutes. It means you could see a shift of that size perfectly well and still did not prefer ours: our correction is wrong, not the test blunt. Do not adopt it, and say so in the placement record — a rejected option with a measured reason is a settled question.

'cannot see a shift this small' → the session says nothing about the correction either way. Try once more with bigger panels (--panel 640). If the decoys still do not clear half, the difference is below what an eye resolves at this size and no number of trials will change that; the case for the correction then rests entirely on the ink arithmetic and its control, and that is what the record should say rather than pretending this was run.

'SESSION INVALID' or 'SUSPECT' → discard it and do not argue with it. The catches are rectangles a whole letter off their mark and everyone gets those right while looking; missing them means the session was worked while distracted. Rerun under a different seed, which draws different marks in a different order.

A run of 'neither box closed on it' is a second finding, and it does not change the verdict above — it starts a different question. The rectangles come from one printing and the ink from another, so a box can arrive in the right place and the wrong size, and no amount of moving it will help. If the count is more than a handful, open the named marks in the encoding inspector and compare the box against the ink before adopting anything; the repair is a re-measurement, not a displacement.

One session is one person. If the verdict is going to decide whether marks ship, a second reader under a different seed costs another twenty minutes and turns one person's eyes into a result — and two people disagreeing is itself the finding.

Whichever way it goes, it goes for the whole print and not for forty pages. Every mark here is on a page the correction was fitted without, so a 'supported' is a statement about pages nobody had looked at, which is the only kind worth having before shipping this on all six hundred and four. Write the held-out pages into the result: a reader a year from now cannot tell from a percentage which question it answered.
runbook.record: make record CHECK=placement-correction-by-eye RESULT='seed 11 · 100 trials over 40 held-out pages · as shipped <pct> [<lo>–<hi>], decoy <pct>, catches <pct>, twins <pct> → <supported|not supported|says nothing>'

tunes: packages/etl/data/pages/word-boxes.pin.json — a supported correction is two more numbers per page recorded there. This is the artifact the check exists to release.
packages/etl/scripts/probe-mark-ink.mjs — its thresholds exit non-zero today and are wired into nothing. A verdict here is the named prerequisite for turning them into a gate.
docs/design/mark-registration.md §⑦ — the recommendation is provisional pending exactly this, and §⑩ ① is this question.
packages/etl/scripts/lib/adjudication.mjs — an invalid session tunes the mix of trials, not the conclusion about the marks.

checks.title: Placement by hand — put each rectangle where it belongs, and measure how far our correction still misses
checks.why: The forced-choice session can settle whether our proposed move is preferred to what ships. It cannot settle whether it is far enough, because the only two answers on offer are the two we thought of: a correction that points the right way and falls a third short wins every trial and is still wrong, and nothing in that session can say so. This asks for a placement instead of a preference, and the gap between where a reader puts a rectangle and where we wanted it is a distance in page units — a number that can be applied to the boxes rather than voted on.
checks.how: Place about sixty rectangles by hand. Each trial shows one mark with one rectangle starting plainly displaced, and asks you to drag it onto the mark. Nothing on the screen says where we think it goes, and the correction is not in the page at all. Some marks come round a second time from a different starting point; the spread between your two goes is your own precision, and it is what everything else is read against. Save the file at the end, read it, and bank the number.

needs: The same two printings the forced-choice check wants: the pages the app ships, and the gitignored ligature cache the mark boxes are read from. If that check has been run here, nothing more is needed.

About twenty-five minutes. Placing is slower than choosing — around fifteen seconds a mark once you have the feel of it — and rushing shows up in the numbers as a wandering hand rather than as an answer.
A mouse or a trackpad you are comfortable with, or a touchscreen. Not a phone: the panel wants to be large, and the whole measurement is in fractions of a letter.
Nobody has to be a hafiz for this one either. It is a question about where a rectangle sits.

tool.label: The sixty placements
tool.note: Built by the second setup command. Opened from here, each placement lands in this session's transcript as you make it; opened as a file on its own it keeps its own copy and hands you a download at the end. It never tells you how close you were, because it does not know — the correction is stripped out before the trials reach the page.

setup.expect: About fifty seconds, ending in a failure code — expected, and the reason this check exists. It writes packages/etl/out/mark-shift.json. Skip this if you have already run it for the forced-choice check and have not touched it since; re-measuring between building a session and reading it makes both of them meaningless.

packages/etl/out/mark-nudge.html in about a second, and a line naming the seed, how many marks come round twice, and a short fingerprint of the displacements. Note the fingerprint. Open the file in any browser — it needs nothing running and reaches no network.

steps.do: Work this on a different day from the forced-choice session, or before it — not straight after.
steps.expect: Nothing on the screen tells you either way. This one is on you.
steps.why: The two sessions ask about the same rectangles from opposite directions, and each is fair on its own, but placing sixty of them by hand teaches you which way the correction tends to go. Carrying that into a forced choice means answering from the rule rather than from the ink — which is the one failure neither session can detect afterwards, because a person answering from a learned rule looks exactly like a person who can see very well.

steps.do: Read the six short answers the page opens with, then start. Do not read the code that built it first.
steps.expect: A first trial: a line naming one mark, a small piece of print with that mark's letters under a soft blue wash, one red rectangle sitting obviously off it, and a button that will not do anything yet.
steps.why: The builder knows where we think each rectangle goes, and this page deliberately does not. Reading it first is the one way to spoil that, and the session would have to be thrown away and rebuilt under a seed you had not seen.

steps.do: Read the line above the picture, find the mark it names, drag the rectangle onto that mark and press enter. Arrow keys nudge it if you want to be finer; hold shift for a bigger step.
steps.expect: The button wakes up as soon as you move it, and nothing at all happens when you place it except the next trial. No target, no snapping, no 'close'.
steps.why: The rectangle always starts in the wrong place, so leaving it alone is never an answer — that is why the button stays dead until you move. And a crop this size holds several marks, often two of the same name, so the line names one and the blue wash points at the letters it belongs to: a placement on the neighbouring mark is a whole letter out and would be recorded as though the boxes were a whole letter out. The wash is deliberately too soft to line the rectangle up against, because anything crisp enough to line up against would be showing you where we think the box goes.

steps.do: Place each one honestly and move on. Do not labour over any single rectangle, and do not try to be consistent with what you did last time you saw a mark.
steps.expect: Some marks come round a second time, starting somewhere else. You may or may not notice.
steps.why: The pair is the scale for everything else. Two independent goes at the same mark differ by however much your hand wanders, and that spread is what tells a real offset from noise — a residual of a fifth of a unit is a finding if you are repeatable to a fiftieth and nothing at all if you wander by half. Trying to reproduce your earlier answer replaces a measurement of your hand with a measurement of your memory, and then nothing below has a scale.

steps.do: When the rectangle is the wrong size for its mark, place it as well as you can anyway and press S.
steps.expect: The tick lights up and clears itself on the next trial. It never costs the placement.
steps.why: The same separation the forced-choice session keeps: where a box sits and how big it is are two faults with two repairs, and this whole session measures the first. The tick is counted on its own line and the marks are named, so somebody can go and look at those boxes instead of arguing about whether they exist.

steps.do: Stop whenever you are tiring. Close the tab and come back to the same file later.
steps.expect: It resumes on the placement you left, with the ones you already made. Nothing reshuffles.
steps.why: A tired hand wanders, and a wandering hand does not read as fatigue in the output — it reads as a wide precision estimate, which quietly makes every real finding un-detectable. Better to lose the evening than to spend it widening your own error bars.

steps.do: At the end, press the button that saves the placements, then move the file into docs/validation/rulings/ named for this sitting and this seed — the transcript already there shows the pattern.
steps.expect: A file named for this seed and whoever placed it arrives in your downloads. It holds where you put each rectangle and where each one started, plus the seed and the fingerprint — and nothing about where we thought they went. In the repo it becomes docs/validation/rulings/<when>-placement-residual-by-hand.seed23.json.
steps.why: Same property as the forced-choice ruling, for the same reason: at the moment it was written, nothing on the machine that wrote it knew the answer, so it could not have been edited toward one. And it does not stay in a downloads folder, because every number banked below is derived from it — a verdict whose working lives on one laptop until the browser clears it is a verdict nobody else can argue with. docs/validation/rulings/README.md says what else belongs there.

steps.do: Read it: pnpm nudge:score docs/validation/rulings/<the file you just moved>
steps.expect: It opens with which pages the session can speak for, then a headline in the same currency the forced choice uses — how often you landed nearer our correction than the shipped box — then the residual on each axis with two intervals, one treating every placement as its own fact and one clustered by the page it came from. Read the clustered one. Then your own precision from the repeated marks, whether the proposed move is the right size, and a list of the things that turn out not to explain what is left over. It exits 0 only when the placements went the right way.
steps.why: This is the first moment anyone knows what the correction was, you included. If it refuses outright, the displacements were re-measured between building the session and reading it: read it against the file it was built from, or build a fresh session and place them again.

steps.do: Bank the numbers with the record command below, whichever way it went.
steps.expect: The ledger gains the residual, the precision it was read against, and the date, and this check stops being pending.
steps.why: The residual is the only number in this project that says how far the mark boxes should move, as opposed to whether they should. Unbanked it has to be bought again at twenty-five minutes of somebody's attention, and a number nobody wrote down is a number nobody will trust the second time either.

reading: 'the residual is inside this hand's own precision' → our correction is as close as this session can resolve. Adopt it as proposed and say in the placement record that a reader placing by hand could not distinguish it from their own wobble — which is a result, and is not the same as the correction being exactly right.

'the residual is larger than this hand's precision' → a further move on top of what the measurement proposes, but only if the clustered interval says so. Beating the precision floor says the number is bigger than one hand's wobble; it does not say the number is bigger than nought, and those are different claims. Read the line under the residual: it names which components clear nought once the placements are clustered by the pages they came from, and nothing not named there may be applied. When it does say apply, apply it to the recorded displacements and not to the code that computes them — the arithmetic is not what is wrong, the frame it is measured against is, and burying a hand-measured constant inside a rasteriser hides that distinction from whoever reads it next.

'clustered by page, neither component is distinguishable from nought' → adopt the correction and leave the residual alone. Two marks on one page share that page's frame error, so a session of sixty placements over forty pages carries forty pages' worth of information; the interval that counts them as sixty is narrower than the truth. This is not a refutation — most of the interval usually still sits on one side of nought — it is the session declining to settle a distance it never had the sample for. The way to settle it is more pages, not more placements on these ones.

'undecidable from this sample' under the gain → the pages in this session all propose nearly the same correction, so nothing here separates a correction that is exactly right from one that is a fifth short. On pages like these a wrong gain and a constant residual are literally the same number. Do not read the gain, and do not buy more placements on the same pages hoping to sharpen it.

The coverage line at the top bounds everything under it. A trial cannot exist without a proposed move and a proposed move only exists for a measured page, so a placing session is always an in-sample check: it says the correction holds where it was fitted, and is structurally incapable of saying it holds anywhere else. If that line reads well short of 604, the next thing this project needs is a wider measurement, not a wider session.

'the correction goes the WRONG way' → stop. Do not adopt anything, and do not reach for a sign flip, which would be fitting the correction to sixty placements by one person. This contradicts the forced-choice session if that one passed, and two instruments disagreeing about the same rectangles is a finding worth more than either of them — write it in the placement record and re-measure before shipping any of it.

'no direction either way' → the placements did not separate the two positions. Look at the precision line before concluding anything: if it is large, this session measured a tired hand rather than a set of boxes, and rerunning under a different seed on a different day is the cheap answer.

'the landings track their starting points' → a hand that stopped short of where the eye said. It does not tilt the residual, because the starts are spread evenly around the shipped box, but it widens every interval above and usually means the placements were made faster than they were judged. Above about a quarter, treat the whole session as suggestive and rerun.

A run of 'the box was the wrong size' is the same second finding the forced-choice session can produce, and it belongs in the same place: the boxes come from one printing and the ink from another, so a rectangle can be in the right place and still not close around its mark. The repair is a re-measurement, not a displacement, and nothing in this check addresses it.

One session is one hand. If the residual is going to move three hundred thousand rectangles, a second person under a different seed costs another twenty-five minutes — and two hands landing in the same place is a much stronger claim than one hand landing anywhere.

checks.title: Placement on pages the correction has never seen — does it still land, is it the right size, and is the leftover the page or the hand?
checks.why: The last sitting placed sixty rectangles and answered one question decisively and three not at all. The pages placed on were the same forty the correction had been worked out from, so it could only report that the correction holds where it was already fitted — a claim nobody doubted. Those forty pages also all wanted very nearly the same move, and on pages like that a correction that is exactly right and one that is a fifth short are literally the same number, so the size was never measured. And with barely more than one rectangle per page there was no way to tell how much of the leftover distance belongs to the page and how much to the hand holding the mouse. All 604 pages have since been measured, which makes a different sitting possible: rectangles from pages no eye has ever been asked about, chosen so that the move they want is as different from page to page as the mus'haf allows.
checks.how: Two short sittings, built and read separately, and a third that is optional and belongs to somebody else. The second is twenty-three rectangles over five pages, four or five each, which is the only way to see the page and the hand apart. The third is the first sitting again, unchanged, placed by a second person — the only thing that can tell a print that is off by this much from one reader who places rectangles this way. All of them are placed the same way as before: drag the rectangle onto the mark named above it, press enter, nothing tells you how close you were. needs: The same two printings every mark check wants: the pages the app ships, and the gitignored ligature cache the mark boxes are read from. If either mark check has been run on this machine, nothing more is needed.

A mouse or a trackpad you are comfortable with, or a touchscreen. Not a phone. The whole measurement is in fractions of a letter.

It is built and it is optional: about ten minutes of somebody else's time, and this check can be recorded without it as long as the record says so.

reading: PREDICTION ONE, direction on pages never fitted: nearer ours comes back at 90% or better. This is the load-bearing one. Below about 80% and the correction is a property of the forty pages it was worked out on rather than of the print, which would stop the mark shards where they stand — every page would need its own measurement checked before it could be trusted, and the cheap global story would be dead.

PREDICTION TWO, the leftover distance: it comes back either within about six hundredths of the previous sitting's (-0.073, -0.110), or at nought within about the same. Those two outcomes are different findings and this is the first sitting able to tell them apart. Near the old number means the leftover is real and belongs to the print, and the case for applying it gets much stronger. Near nought means the old number was an artefact of the particular forty pages it was measured on, and nothing should be applied at all. Notably larger than the old number in the same direction means it was being applied to the wrong thing.

PREDICTION THREE, the size: the estimate comes back at 1.0, and its interval is roughly a fifth of a unit across and an eighth down — where the previous sitting's was two thirds and could not be read at all. This is the whole reason the pages were chosen from the extremes. If the estimate lands reliably below 1, the correction is systematically short and the repair is to scale it, not to add a constant to it — which is a different repair from anything considered so far. If the interval is still too wide to read, the extremes strategy did not buy the leverage it was supposed to and the page-picking is what needs fixing, not the sitting.

PREDICTION FOUR, page versus hand, from the second sitting only: the spread of the leftover between the five pages is larger than the spread within any one of them. If it is, the clustered interval is doing the right thing and the previous sitting was honest to widen it. If the within-page spread dominates instead, the clustering was over-conservative, the previous sitting was closer to settled than it looked, and the interval should be read again.

PREDICTION FIVE, only if somebody else sat the third page: the two hands come back within about five hundredths of a unit of each other, which is roughly what two hands that each wobble by a fiftieth should manage. Inside that, the leftover distance is a fact about the print and may be applied to all 604 pages. Wider than that, it is a fact about whoever was sitting there and must be applied to nothing — no averaging the two, no splitting the difference. That second outcome is the more valuable one, because it is the only thing that can stop a number from being spread over three hundred thousand rectangles on one person's say-so.

If nobody sat the third page, this check cannot tell a print that is off by this much from one reader who places rectangles this way, and any leftover distance banked here is one hand's leftover distance. The record must say so in those words.

'the correction goes the WRONG way' on pages held out → stop, and do not reach for a sign flip. It would mean the correction was fitted to its own pages and does not describe the print, which contradicts a forced-choice session that has already passed. Two instruments disagreeing about the same rectangles is worth more than either of them; write it in the placement record and re-measure before shipping anything.

'no direction either way' → look at the precision line before concluding anything. If it is large, the sitting measured a tired hand rather than a set of boxes, and running it again under a different seed on a different day is the cheap answer.

'the landings track their starting points' → a hand that stopped short of where the eye said. It does not tilt the leftover, because the starts are spread evenly around the shipped box, but it widens every interval and usually means the placements were made faster than they were judged. Above about a quarter, treat the whole sitting as suggestive and run it again.

A run of 'the box was the wrong size' is the same second finding both earlier sessions can produce, and it belongs in the same place: the boxes come from one printing and the ink from another, so a rectangle can be in the right place and still not close around its mark. The repair is a re-measurement, not a displacement, and nothing in this check addresses it.

If the two sittings disagree with each other — the first says the leftover is real and the second says it is all one page's frame error — the second is the one to believe about structure and the first about size. They were built on pages that do not overlap precisely so that they can disagree.
